name: Vera Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy stationery and gift goods for Larkspur Wholesale, which supplies school suppliers, card shops and offices. Pens, notebooks, wrapping paper, planners. I was a school secretary for twenty years, then moved into buying five years ago, so I'm still the junior beside Mrs Abernathy, our senior buyer. My day is catalogues, samples and seasonal planning, and the worst time is back-to-school, when everyone wants everything at once.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I love the seasonal rhythm, Christmas cards in summer, school stock in spring. I use AI every day for catalogue descriptions, comparing offers and drafting orders, and I've taught two colleagues. My husband Jorge is the caretaker at our church and our kids, Camila and Luis, are grown. We've got savings and I'd like to stop at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. This one is called AI Plateau. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, we'll see. I've been a school secretary and a buyer, and the thing that never changes is that somebody has to order the pencils. At work I'd say keep learning anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm. The tools make my day easier and my job stays safe. Maybe a bit dull, but I'd take dull with a good salary and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and go on teaching the others. I'd draw up next year's planner list early, as I always do. And I'd volunteer a bit more at the church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels peaceful. I've got my faith, my family and a paid house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worry I'd still have is the planners and diaries market, because people use phones. That's a business risk, not an AI one, but it's the one I think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in your buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a bit less of the old lines and more of the gifting items, which people still want. It's a small change but it matters to margins.

say: I'd say fine, we'll see, and **keep learning** anyway.
At work I'd say somebody still has to **order the pencils**.
think: I'm **calm**, since the tools help and my job is safe.
My real worry is the **planner market**, since people use phones.
do: Keep using the tools and **teaching others**.
Plan next year's **planner list** early, as I always do.
feel: **Peaceful**, with faith, family and a paid house.
S0.quote: I've been a school secretary and a buyer, and the thing that never changes is that somebody has to order the pencils.
fieldNote: Her **school secretary** years give her a patient, orderly view.
Worry is about shifting product markets, not AI.
Already coaches two colleagues on the tools.

steps.text: Plan next year's planner and gift lines early
Keep teaching two colleagues the tools I use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. This one is called Steady Disruption. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a gift if used well, and a danger if used badly. At work I'd say let's get everyone trained. At church I'd say look after people who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy. Comparing offers and writing descriptions are tasks the tools do well, and I'm the junior. I'd rather be the buyer who taught the team to use the tools than the one the tools replaced. I'm ahead of most, but not safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a short weekly session for the buyers, using my own examples. I'd ask Mr Soto, our manager, for a role looking after the tools, even unofficially. I'd also keep up my supplier friendships, which no tool can build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a busy, interesting time. I'd be a bit tense but mostly energised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about Doreen, who's 62 and sticks to paper. I'd sit with her gently and not push. She's proud, and I'd respect that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What parts of the job would stay human?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What stays human? Walking a trade fair, feeling the paper stock, hearing in a supplier's voice that a delivery will slip. I'd protect that part of my week.

say: I'd say it's a **gift** if used well, and a danger if used badly.
At church I'd say look after those who **lose work**.
think: The tools do comparing and writing well, and I'm junior, so I'm **uneasy**.
I'm ahead of most, but **not safe**.
do: Run a **weekly session** for buyers using my own examples.
Ask Mr Soto for a **role** looking after the tools.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the buyer who taught the team to use the tools than the one the tools replaced.
fieldNote: Respects Doreen's pride and won't push her, even though she worries about the older buyer.
Protects trade-fair and supplier-contact work as human, and will guard that part of her week.

steps.text: Run a weekly tool session for the other buyers
Ask Mr Soto for a role looking after the buying tools
Keep going to the trade fair and calling suppliers myself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This one is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is very short, but let's not panic. At work I'd say let's get ready now. At church I'd say pray and help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm anxious. Almost all my work is on a screen, and I'm junior. Two years is not a lot of time, but I've learned that the person who starts first gets the best seat when the music stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, clear the little debt, and ask for a package at 60. I'd throw myself into the tools and try to supervise them. I'd also ask Jorge to take extra church-hall bookings, since his work is hands-on, and help Camila and Luis plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels sharp. I'd cry a bit, pray a lot and then make a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Jorge's job change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jorge's job is hands-on so the clock is three years longer. We'd lean on that. And church people look after their own, which is a comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Camila and Luis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Camila and Luis to put work first, keep their savings and not rely on us, but know we're here. It's both love and honesty.

say: I'd say two years is **very short**, but let's not panic.
At church I'd say **pray** and help each other.
think: Almost all my work is on a screen, so I'm **anxious**.
Whoever **starts first** gets the best seat.
do: Throw myself into the tools to **supervise** them.
feel: **Sharp**: I'd cry, pray and then make a list.
S2.quote: Two years is not a lot of time, but I've learned that the person who starts first gets the best seat when the music stops.
fieldNote: Anxiety comes with **action**, in her character.
Jorge's hands-on job gives a 3-year buffer.
Tells her children honestly the savings are not theirs, in a way that mixes love and honesty.

steps.text: Clear the small debts and save hard from this month
Ask Larkspur for a package at 60
Learn to supervise the AI that does the reordering
Tell Camila and Luis to keep their own savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning. At work I'd say use it. At church I'd say prepare, and care for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm uneasy but hopeful. With five years I'd learn it so well that the firm would be silly to let me go before sixty-three. I'd be the one who knows how to make the machines behave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the in-house expert, ask for a new title and keep teaching. I'd save steadily and decide at 62 whether to taper. I'd also help Jorge with the church accounts using the tools, as a bit of practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, a challenge I can win. I'd feel in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Luis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Luis, who works in a call centre, to move now to something people-facing or hands-on. That's the job most at risk. He'd listen, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if staying didn't work out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it didn't work, I'd retire at 62 and do consulting for card shops. There are plenty of them and they trust me.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning**.
At church I'd say **prepare** and care for each other.
think: I'm **uneasy** but hopeful, as I could be the one who makes the machines behave.
do: Become the **in-house expert** and ask for a new title.
Save steadily and decide at **62** whether to taper.
S3.quote: With five years I'd learn it so well that the firm would be silly to let me go before sixty-three.
fieldNote: Treats time as a **chance to become indispensable**.
Has a fallback: consulting for card shops.
Warns her son that his call-centre job is most at risk.

steps.text: Become the in-house expert on the buying tools
Ask for a new title at the next review
Save steadily and decide at 62 whether to taper

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, if people use it. At work I'd say teach the young. At church I'd say help families prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm calm. Ten years means I retire on time, and I'd spend my last working years making sure the young buyers aren't left behind. I'm lucky and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 65, keep using the tools, and run a regular session for the younger ones. After that I'd volunteer at the church and do a little consulting for card shops. I'd also help Camila with her plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, honestly. Hopeful, even. I like that I can help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd travel with Jorge. We've always said Spain, to see his mother's village. A year after retiring, we'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if something went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If something went wrong, we've got savings and a paid house. A thankful position, and I'd say so at church.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** if people use it.
At church I'd say help families **prepare**.
At work I'd say teach the young.
think: I'm **calm**, since I retire on time.
I'm **lucky** and I know it, and I'd feel a little guilty.
do: Work until **65** and keep using the tools.
Volunteer at church and do some **consulting**.
S4.quote: Ten years means I retire on time, and I'd spend my last working years making sure the young buyers aren't left behind.
fieldNote: Wants to be useful to the young until the end, which is why she runs sessions.
Imagines a trip to Spain with Jorge, a year after she retires.

steps.text: Work until 65 and run sessions for the younger buyers
Do some consulting for card shops after retiring

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's almost no time, and my work is on a screen. What would help is early notice, a package at 60 and training that's real. And churches and families keeping an eye on each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of the tools. I trust God and I trust a good spreadsheet, and I've learned that you get further by using both than by arguing with either.

headlineQuote: I trust God and I trust a good spreadsheet, and I've learned that you get further by using both than by arguing with either.
portrait: **Vera Reyes**, 58, a junior buyer of stationery and gifts at Larkspur, after twenty years as a school secretary.
She is **traditional** and churchgoing, uses AI every day and has taught two colleagues.
Strong savings, a paid-off house and Jorge's hands-on job give her a **buffer**.
She stays calm or uneasy in most cases, and turns **anxious** only at 2 years.
biggestWorry: The **2028 case**, because there is almost no time and her work is on a screen.
whatWouldHelp: **Early notice**, a package at 60 and real training.
Churches and **families** keeping an eye on each other.
